content.title: About
content.content: Fruit flavored drink is a non‑alcoholic refreshing beverage made from natural fruit juices, water and a modest amount of sugar or sweeteners. It offers a bright fruit taste, light carbonation and low calorie content, making it a popular choice for quenching thirst.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Most fruit drinks combine several juice varieties to create a more complex flavor profile.
Some brands use cold‑press technology to retain more vitamins and aromatic compounds.
Fruit drinks are often fortified with vitamin C and other antioxidants to boost nutritional value.
Carbonated versions add a bubbly sensation that enhances flavor perception.
In certain markets fruit drinks are sold in glass bottles to emphasize a premium image.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Citrus and berry juices provide a substantial amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The majority of the drink is water, helping to maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: With moderate sugar content or the use of sweeteners, the beverage is relatively low in calories, suitable for weight management.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Some fruit drinks contain small amounts of dietary fiber that can aid normal bowel function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Fruit extracts are rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Certain versions may contain high levels of sugar, which is undesirable for people with diabetes or those monitoring calorie intake.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Acidic drinks can irritate the stomach lining and erode tooth enamel with frequent consumption.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Flavors, preservatives or other additives may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Preservatives and artificial additives
items.content: Some brands use preservatives that may be unwanted by consumers seeking clean‑label products.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fruit drink chilled, optionally over ice or with fresh fruit slices to enhance flavor. It works well as a standalone refresher or as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard cider is an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting apple juice with yeast. It combines the natural sweetness of apples with a subtle tartness and often a light carbonation. Alcohol content typically ranges from 4 % to 8 % ABV.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hard cider originated in England in the 17th century as a way to preserve apple juice.
In the United States, cider gained popularity in the 1970s as an alternative to beer.
More than 30 apple varieties are used for cider production, each imparting distinct aromas.
Traditional English cider is often aged in oak barrels, adding vanilla notes.
In some regions the term “cider” refers to a non‑alcoholic drink, while “hard cider” distinguishes the alcoholic version.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Apples contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Moderate cider consumption may improve lipid profiles thanks to apple‑derived phytochemicals.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fermentation produces vitamins B2 and B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: A small amount of soluble fiber in cider can aid gut health.

items.title: Lower sugar content
items.content: Compared with many other alcoholic drinks, cider often contains less added sugar.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Cider contains alcohol and should be consumed responsibly; avoid during pregnancy, driving, or with liver disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some ciders are sweetened, increasing calories and affecting blood glucose levels.

items.title: Apple allergy
items.content: People allergic to apples may react to cider.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain drugs, such as sedatives.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve hard cider chilled (6‑8 °C) in a glass or tumbler. It can be enjoyed on its own, used in cocktails, or paired with cheeses, roasted meats, and fruit desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cider in a cool, dark place, preferably refrigerate after opening. Keep the bottle tightly sealed to retain carbonation. Once opened, it is best consumed within 3‑5 days.

rice-brown-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Rice, brown, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole grain that retains its bran layer and germ. When cooked without added fat it keeps most of its nutrients, offers a mild nutty aroma and a slightly chewy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice provides more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
It is a good source of magnesium, which supports muscle and nerve function.
When stored properly, whole grains can keep their quality for up to a year.
In Japan brown rice is traditionally called “genmai,” meaning “whole grain.”
There are several varieties, including long‑grain basmati and medium‑grain arborio.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium participates in over 300 biochemical reactions, including protein synthesis and heart rhythm maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3, and B6 support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white rice, brown rice raises blood glucose more slowly, which is beneficial for weight control and diabetes management.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: The bran layer contains phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Present in the bran, it can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting lowers its level.

items.title: Arsenic
items.content: In some regions soil may be contaminated; choose rice from reputable sources.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: High fiber intake may cause bloating and gas in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked brown rice can be served as a side dish, added to salads, soups, pilafs, and vegetarian meals. It pairs well with legumes, vegetables, and lean proteins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry whole grains in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and kept in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days, or frozen for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Turrnip greens are edible leafy vegetables cultivated in the northern states of the USA. The product is supplied in a ready‑to‑eat form after cooking, which preserves most nutrients and makes it convenient for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turrnip belongs to the Brassicaceae family and is closely related to turnip and radish.
In the United States, turrnip is often used as a spinach substitute in winter dishes.
Cooked turrnip retains over 80 % of its vitamin C, which degrades quickly in raw preparations.
The leaves are rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification processes.
Turrnip is grown in cold climates and is frost‑tolerant.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked turrnip provides a substantial amount of vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in turrnip aids digestion and helps maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal heart function and blood‑pressure regulation.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked turrnip contains fewer than 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Glucosinolates and flavonoids in turrnip have antioxidant activity, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy to cruciferous vegetables
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions such as itching, swelling, or hives after consuming turrnip.

items.title: Oxalic acid content
items.content: Oxalic acid may contribute to kidney‑stone formation in susceptible persons; moderate intake is advised.

items.title: Vitamin C loss over time
items.content: After cooking, vitamin C gradually degrades, so the product should be consumed within 2‑3 days of opening.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turrnip can be added to soups, stews, omelets, or used as a side dish for meat. It also works well mixed into mashed potatoes or chilled in salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turrnip in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
